A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ThinkEval framework and KnowGIC study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across layout changes.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of five editing techniques across three LLMs, the Harry Potter case study, and supplementary model-error analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and adds original IKE results, automated-validation and runtime measurements, annotation agreement, and paraphrasing experiments.

M1.justification: Appendix K.2 introduces an implemented GPT-4o judge variant for intermediate triplet validation and pruning, reserving human effort for final verification. This modifies one workflow component; the original framework and Algorithms 1–3 remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The 1,406-chain KnowGIC corpus and its factual domains remain unchanged. Appendix R adds systematically paraphrased queries as a post-edit testing condition. Extensions to commonsense, procedural, and rule-based knowledge in Appendix I remain proposed future work.

E2.justification: Appendix L and Table 12 add evaluated IKE results across the three retained LLMs, extending the comparison to parameter-preserving editing. IKE was previously discussed but not evaluated. The original five-method comparison remains intact.

E3.justification: Several new evaluation designs are documented: a 100-chain paraphrasing study averaging correctness probabilities over three paraphrases per link, a 250-chain study with three annotators, and five-iteration runtime and automated-judge evaluations. These substantially expand evaluation of the framework itself without revising the retained benchmark protocol.

E4.justification: Appendices K, O, and R add substantial analyses of computational scaling, automated versus human validation, annotation consistency, and sensitivity to query phrasing. The earlier Harry Potter case study and Qwen knowledge-gap analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix O newly reports inter-annotator reliability using approximately 97% raw agreement and 98% Gwet’s AC1. The five-response case-study protocol already appeared in v2; v3 does not introduce seed-based uncertainty estimates or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and case-study values remain unchanged, including every Table 4 entry. New results include IKE IFR scores of 0.542, 0.756, and 0.247 for GPT2-XL, Llama3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively, plus runtime, judge accuracy, annotation agreement, and paraphrasing results. Table 16 uses a different subset and query procedure, so its scores are not same-setting performance changes.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds an explicit qualification that graph reasoning does not assume transitive closure and retains paths only when they plausibly imply a meaningful subject–object relationship. Definitions 1–4 and the metric equations remain unchanged. Appendix J illustrates the existing IFR calculation rather than introducing a new derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: ThinkEval, deep editing, IFR, KnowGIC, and the trade-off between indirect leakage and contextual preservation. The appendix additions do not materially redefine these main contributions.

C2.justification: New appendices substantially expand interpretation of practical reliability: normalization is presented as mitigating model bias, automation as reducing human effort, and paraphrasing results as establishing stability. They also discuss possible non-factual applications and future editing objectives. Some new interpretations, particularly unchanged rankings in Appendix R, exceed the reported evidence.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the anonymous dataset link with a named GitHub repository and adds exact model identifiers, clarification of unmodified checkpoints and default editing configurations, alias-based validation details, and operational timings. It also states that new study materials are released. The original GPU specification, algorithms, and prompt templates were already documented.

R1.justification: v3 adds five works, including Gao’s consistency studies, SpecialtyScribe, and two Wang papers, and expands the comparison with MQuAKE in Appendix Q. Numerous other reference changes update publication metadata for already cited works rather than introducing new research positioning.

P1.justification: The main sections and existing appendices remain largely verbatim. Changes include author and affiliation presentation, limited wording edits, and additional explanatory sections such as the worked IFR example and workflow clarification. The existing narrative and section order remain stable.

P2.justification: Tables 9–16 substantially expand the empirical and explanatory displays, covering calculation examples, validation, costs, IKE, reliability, workflow roles, and paraphrasing. Figures 1–22 are retained, while several appendix graphs are resized and regrouped and other material reflows.

improvement.justification: v3 adds useful checks on annotation, automation, and query phrasing, extends evaluation to IKE, and improves operational documentation. These address practical questions largely untested in v2. The gain is limited: Appendix R claims stable rankings despite changed orderings in Tables 4 and 16 and does not report a matching unmodified-query subset control. Appendix K also leaves its query counts and runtime totals unreconciled. The added evidence improves usefulness, while the stronger reliability conclusions remain insufficiently supported.
